steps.eyebrow: Browser same-origin policy and the CORS/authentication boundary
steps.title: Establish the rule

blocks.text: For a browser page calling an API, separate address matching from permission to access the endpoint.
An origin combines scheme, host and port. A difference in any one makes URLs cross-origin.
Browser restrictions limit a script’s access to cross-origin responses unless the server permits it through CORS. The API must independently check endpoint access.
https://shop.example:443/orders and https://shop.example:443/items share an origin despite different paths. Changing the host to api.example or the port to 8443 makes the call cross-origin.
Browser permission to read a response is not authentication. The API still needs its own access checks.

blocks.text: Choose an order operation’s method by its intended effect, not by a convenient label.
Safe methods request essentially read-only semantics. Incidental logging does not make them unsafe.

Idempotency means identical repetition has the same intended server effect as one request, even if replies differ. GET retrieves a representation; HEAD has the same semantics without response content. Both are safe and idempotent. POST requests resource-specific processing and is not generally idempotent. PUT creates or replaces target state; DELETE removes its association with current functionality. Both are idempotent, not safe.

left.alt_text: GET retrieves a representation and HEAD requests the same semantics without response content; both map to safe and idempotent.

nodes.label: PUT: create or replace target state
POST: resource-specific processing; not generally idempotent

right.alt_text: PUT creates or replaces target state and DELETE removes its association; both map to idempotent, not safe. POST requests resource-specific processing and is not generally idempotent.

blocks.takeaway: Safety and idempotency are separate properties.

blocks.text: Reading an order and replacing it can both be idempotent, but only reading is safe. Repeated PUT requests the same target state; POST processing is not generally idempotent. Describe the requested change and identical repetition separately. Matching replies are not the test.

At /orders/42, GET retrieves a representation and HEAD requests the same semantics without content. Logging is incidental. Repeating a PUT replacement requests the same target state, even if replies differ. Repeated DELETE also need not return identical replies. POST collection processing is not generally idempotent. Ask separately: does this request a change, and does identical repetition preserve the intended effect?
Safety does not prohibit all incidental effects. Idempotency does not require identical replies. PUT and DELETE can be idempotent yet unsafe.
An order’s outgoing body format, preferred response format and actual response format are separate information.
Content-Type labels the media type of its associated representation, not the preferred response format.

Accept lists acceptable response media types. For JSON content, send Content-Type: application/json; request a JSON response with Accept: application/json. Inspect the reply’s Content-Type separately.
In this JSON exchange, the request Content-Type labels the submitted content. Accept states the response preference. Read the response’s own Content-Type to identify what came back.
Content-Type labels content. Accept carries the client’s response preference.

blocks.text: Two order drafts need independent items, even though they share the class’s behavior.
A class statement creates a class with methods defining behavior. Calling that class creates an instance.

__init__(self, ...) initializes an instance; self.attribute stores its state. An instance method receives that instance first. Instance variables are specific to each instance; class variables are shared. For independent mutable values, create a fresh value on self inside __init__.

nodes.label: Alternative: one mutable class items shared by both

steps.eyebrow: Python classes and instances for service models
steps.title: Why the distinction matters

blocks.text: Change only draft_a’s items and inspect draft_b. Calling Draft twice does not fix shared mutable class state. Assign a fresh collection to self during initialization. Shared methods use self to identify the instance being changed.

blocks.text: Draft defines behavior; draft_a and draft_b are instances. A fresh self.items in each __init__ gives each draft its own collection. One mutable items value on the class can instead be shared. Follow ownership: the method’s first argument identifies the instance, not a new copy of every attribute.
Two instances can still share a mutable class variable. Initialize fresh mutable state on self when independence is required.

To add the supplied item only to the first draft, write `draft_a.items.append(item)`. The list's `append(value)` method adds one value to that list. Because each initializer creates a fresh `self.items = []`, `draft_a.items` then contains the item while `draft_b.items` remains empty.

tiles.title: Context-managed resource cleanup · Cooperative concurrency with async and await

blocks.text: File-reading work may fail. Mark cleanup on both normal and exceptional exit.
Use with manager as resource: and an indented block to enter a managed resource scope.

After __enter__ succeeds, __exit__ runs on normal or exceptional block exit. It receives exception details and can suppress an exception by returning true; cleanup alone does not imply suppression. with open(...) as file closes the file after the block, even on an exception.

nodes.label: General __exit__: true may suppress; cleanup alone does not

blocks.alt_text: with open("orders.txt") as file: →     file.read() inside managed scope → Normal exit → file closed → Exception exit → file closed → General __exit__: true may suppress; cleanup alone does not

blocks.text: Mark successful entry, work inside the block and departure. Normal departure and an exception both close the file. For a general manager, a true __exit__ return may suppress an exception, but releasing the resource is a separate decision. A cleanup trace is not proof the work succeeded.

In with open(...) as file, keep reading inside the indented scope. After successful entry, normal exit closes the file; exceptional exit also closes it. A general manager’s __exit__ receives exception details and may suppress by returning true. Ask separately whether cleanup occurred and whether the exception propagated.
Successful entry guarantees an exit call, not disappearing exceptions. Cleanup and suppression are separate.

steps.eyebrow: Cooperative concurrency with async and await
steps.title: Establish the rule

blocks.text: Trace actual suspension in an asynchronous task; counting await keywords is not enough.
Calling async def creates a coroutine. Awaiting it runs it and returns its result on completion.

The event loop cooperatively runs one task at a time. While a task waits on a pending future, other tasks may run; completion lets the suspended coroutine resume. An immediately completing await need not suspend. asyncio.sleep suspends the current task, even with delay zero.

nodes.label: Await immediate work: may not suspend
Await pending future: suspend; other tasks may run

blocks.alt_text: Call async function: coroutine created; Await: coroutine runs; Await immediate work: may not suspend; Await pending future: suspend; other tasks may run; Future completes: task resumes; await asyncio.sleep(0): suspends

steps.eyebrow: Cooperative concurrency with async and await
steps.title: Why the distinction matters

blocks.text: An immediately completing await leaves no pending wait requiring a handover. Waiting on a pending future gives another runnable task an opportunity to run; completion lets the first resume. This does not establish which task runs next. asyncio.sleep(0) still suspends.

steps.eyebrow: Cooperative concurrency with async and await

blocks.text: In task_a, calling immediate creates a coroutine; awaiting it runs it and obtains its result. If it completes immediately, no suspension is required. Awaiting pending_io can suspend until its future completes, after which task_a resumes. await asyncio.sleep(0) explicitly suspends. Mark those distinctions without promising an exact interleaving.
An await is not proof that another task ran. Immediate work may finish without suspension; asyncio.sleep suspends even at zero delay.

A decorator can add behavior around a service callable without rewriting that callable.
At function definition, the decorator expression is evaluated and called with the function object. Its returned value becomes the function name’s binding.

@decorate above def function(...): is roughly function = decorate(function). Build a callable wrapper by defining an inner function that calls the supplied function, then returning the inner function.

steps.eyebrow: Isolated Python environments and compatible dependency installation
steps.title: Establish the rule

blocks.text: Two projects can need different dependency versions. Identify which interpreter and packages each uses.
A virtual environment has a particular Python installation and its own installed packages, allowing applications to use different dependency versions.

Create it with python -m venv .venv. Activate using source .venv/bin/activate on Unix or .venv\Scripts\activate on Windows. Install with python -m pip install package; inspect version and location with python -m pip show package. Confirm the interpreter path with which python on Unix or where python on Windows.

blocks.takeaway: Package versions may match while interpreter paths and package locations remain separate.

tiles.title: ASGI server and application request lifecycle

steps.eyebrow: ASGI server and application request lifecycle
steps.title: Establish the rule

blocks.text: The network server and Python application have different roles. ASGI connects them through protocol events.
The ASGI server handles the network connection and invokes the application callable through ASGI.

The callable is async def app(scope, receive, send). scope describes the connection; receive and send exchange events. Receive http.request through receive(), then send http.response.start with status and headers, followed by http.response.body through send().

blocks.alt_text: ASGI server: network connection; Invoke async app(scope, receive, send); scope: connection description; receive(): http.request; send(): http.response.start (status, headers); send(): http.response.body

steps.eyebrow: ASGI server and application request lifecycle
steps.title: Why the distinction matters

blocks.text: Keep scope separate from events: it describes the connection, while receive and send exchange events. Send response status and headers in http.response.start before the http.response.body event. The server owns network handling; the application participates through the ASGI callable.

steps.eyebrow: ASGI server and application request lifecycle
steps.title: Reason through an example

blocks.text: Trace the server invoking app with scope, receive and send. The application receives http.request, sends http.response.start containing status and headers, then sends http.response.body. Draw separate arrows for metadata and body, not one handler return. Keep the network connection in the server box.
The application does not directly own all network handling. The ASGI server handles the connection and invokes the callable.

Pass an event dictionary to `send`. Its `type` names the event. A response-start event carries `status` and `headers`; a response-body event carries `body`. Use the supplied values without choosing a status or implementing networking.

blocks.code:
async def app(scope, receive, send):
    request = await receive()
    await send({'type': 'http.response.start', 'status': supplied_status, 'headers': supplied_headers})
    await send({'type': 'http.response.body', 'body': supplied_body})

annotations.text: `receive()` obtains the supplied request.
Response start precedes response body.

tiles.title: Local password hashing and credential verification without an OAuth password grant

steps.eyebrow: Local password hashing and credential verification without an OAuth password grant
steps.title: Establish the rule

blocks.text: For a local password check, store verification material rather than a password intended to be recovered later.
Use password hashing, not plaintext storage or reversible encryption.

Salts distinguish hashes; an adjustable work factor increases guessing cost. Create pwdlib’s PasswordHash.recommended(), store hash(password), and check submissions with verify(plain_password, stored_hash).

Use the registered synthetic passwords. Create the recommended hasher, store its hash(password) result, then supply the submitted plaintext first and stored hash second to verify. Salt distinguishes hashes; work factor increases guessing cost. Do not replace hashing with reversible storage.
Verification checks a submission against a stored hash. It does not recover the original password through decryption.

blocks.code:
from pwdlib import PasswordHash

password = "synthetic-order-password"
different_password = "different-synthetic-password"
password_hash = PasswordHash.recommended()
stored_hash = password_hash.hash(password)
matching_result = password_hash.verify(password, stored_hash)
nonmatching_result = password_hash.verify(different_password, stored_hash)

annotations.text: Create the recommended hasher and store the hash, not plaintext.
Submitted password first; stored hash second. matching_result is True; nonmatching_result is False. Verification checks the submission without decrypting the stored hash.

blocks.text: For some cross-origin calls, the browser asks permission before sending the intended method and headers.
An OPTIONS preflight asks whether an intended method and headers are permitted. Not every cross-origin request is preflighted.

steps.eyebrow: Choosing HTTP success and failure statuses
steps.title: Establish the rule

blocks.text: Order creation, an absent target and unexpected failure need distinct HTTP outcomes.
The classes are informational 1xx, successful 2xx, redirection 3xx, client error 4xx and server error 5xx.

Use 200 for success, 201 for resource creation and 204 for success without response content. 400 means a perceived request error; 401 lacks valid authentication credentials; 403 refuses fulfillment; 404 does not find or disclose the target; 409 conflicts with current state. 500 denotes an unexpected server condition; 503 temporary inability, such as overload or maintenance.

steps.eyebrow: Choosing HTTP success and failure statuses
steps.title: Why the distinction matters

blocks.text: Choose the outcome class, then its specific meaning. Retrieval differs from creation; missing valid credentials differ from refusal; conflict differs from a target not found or disclosed. Unexpected failure differs from temporary inability. Producing a JSON body does not itself justify a successful status.

steps.eyebrow: Pydantic V2 model construction and input conversion
steps.title: Establish the rule

blocks.text: Order input needs a declared shape. Validation can convert compatible values; it is not merely an original-type check.
Subclass BaseModel and declare typed fields. Construct with Model(field=value, ...) or validate data with Model.model_validate(data).

Compatible inputs can convert to declared types; default validation does not prove their original types matched. Inputs that cannot satisfy the model raise ValidationError with failed-field details. Fields without defaults are required; declared defaults supply omitted values.

annotations.text: quantity required; note default supplied on omission.

Expected outcomes: {'quantity': '3'} and {'quantity': 3} both produce quantity=3 and note=None. {} fails because quantity is required. {'quantity': 'many'} fails integer validation for quantity. Failures raise ValidationError with field details.

Database constraints enforce order integrity even when writes bypass the API.
TYPE NOT NULL rejects nulls independently of the application path.

UNIQUE rejects duplicate combinations; PostgreSQL treats nulls as distinct by default unless NULLS NOT DISTINCT is specified. PRIMARY KEY gives unique non-null row identity and may span columns. FOREIGN KEY requires non-null references to match referenced rows. CHECK constrains row values but passes on true or null; add NOT NULL to reject absence.

blocks.code:
CREATE TABLE orders (
    identity INTEGER,
    customer_reference INTEGER,
    quantity INTEGER NOT NULL,
    external_reference TEXT,
    PRIMARY KEY (identity),
    FOREIGN KEY (customer_reference) REFERENCES customers (identity),
    CHECK (quantity > 0),
    UNIQUE (external_reference)
);

annotations.text: customers already exists with identity as its primary key. PRIMARY KEY may list multiple columns. CHECK passes on true or null, so quantity also needs NOT NULL. UNIQUE preserves PostgreSQL’s default distinct-null behavior; UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT (external_reference) is the alternative when null duplicates must also be rejected.

blocks.text: Inspect proposed orders independently against the baseline. PRIMARY KEY protects unique non-null identity, and FOREIGN KEY checks non-null customer references. quantity needs NOT NULL as well as CHECK. UNIQUE rejects duplicate external references, but PostgreSQL’s default permits distinct nulls; NULLS NOT DISTINCT changes that null comparison. Match each violation to its constraint.
